approachQuestion.prompt:
Calibration Energies

A calibration device supplies an integer array offsets in nondecreasing order. Return a new array containing the square of every offset in nondecreasing order, preserving multiplicity. Do not change offsets.

Constraints: 0 <= n = offsets.length <= 200000; -1000000000 <= offsets[i] <= 1000000000. Each square fits signed 64-bit integers; promote before multiplication. The new array must contain exactly n entries.

Example 1: offsets = [-7,-3,0,2,5] -> [0,4,9,25,49].
Example 2: offsets = [-5,-2,-2] -> [4,4,25].
Example 3: offsets = [] -> [].
constraints: Choose the most efficient valid approach for the entire stated input domain; accept equivalent optimal variants.

options.text: Allocate the returned array of n cells. Compare the squares at the two remaining endpoints, write the larger into the last unfilled cell, and consume that endpoint. On a tie consume either one. Repeat until every input entry is consumed.
options.feedback: The largest square among the remaining sorted values is at an endpoint. Filling from the back preserves order and consumes duplicates separately.

options.text: Create the returned array of all squares, then sort it with a worst-case comparison sort such as heapsort.
options.feedback: This produces the right array for all inputs, but it reorders values by general sorting even though endpoint magnitudes already determine the next output.

options.text: Write the square of each input entry into the corresponding output position and return that array without reordering.
options.feedback: For [-3,-1,2], this returns [9,1,4], which is not nondecreasing.

options.text: Compare the squares of the remaining endpoints, write the smaller into the next output position from the front, and consume that endpoint.
options.feedback: For [-5,-2,1,4], the smallest square 1 is inside. This emits 16 first and cannot produce sorted output.

feedback.reason: Recognize that squaring destroys signed order but the largest remaining magnitude must occur at an endpoint; build the output backward.
details: Allocate the final result array. Compare the two remaining endpoint squares and place the larger into the rightmost unfilled result cell. Consume only the endpoint used, including on a tie. Repeat until the result is full.
Large negative readings may have larger squares than positive readings. Choose between endpoint magnitudes and fill the result backward, where the largest unplaced square belongs.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed after question 1, choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair, with n equal to the original input length. Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed reads, writes, comparisons, and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include every temporary buffer, copy, and call frame. The fixed method is iterative, makes no input copy, uses no hashing, and performs no amortized data-structure operations. Exclude the supplied input and the returned n-cell result array, including its initialization; include allocation and initialization time. The result is filled by indexed writes without resizing.
constraints: Choose the tightest pair for this fixed method, regardless of the approach you selected in question 1.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Consume n readings and write n result cells once.
details: Exactly n input entries are consumed and n output cells are written, so both the upper bound and worst-case lower bound are linear. Result allocation and initialization are also linear. No separate temporary array or recursion is used.

Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed reads, writes, comparisons, and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include every temporary buffer, copy, and call frame. “O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This adds a size-dependent temporary copy or buffer absent from the fixed method.
“O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The method does not restart a full scan for each element; its bounded number of forward or inward scans is linear.
“O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: No sorting or repeated binary searches occur in the fixed method.
